title: Lancers, the blues around 1906 and boogie woogie
summary: Mello describes three-piece dance jobs and the five-part lancers, dates the blues to about 1906, and says boogie woogie is the old colored dance rhythm.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Where the blues came from: Handy, Bolden and early blues

blocks.x: T. Notchie Beg, uh, Lance composed that piece, and that was a real, real nigger piece. I mean, you talk about it as close to being colored. Manny Perez, he's dead in not quite a while, and he told Lance, he says, that was, he says, the most best nigger piece that I ever did here. He says, that really was a nigger piece. I tell you. And I said, oh, he just composed. Lance was pretty good. He was good. I still say, well, we used to have a three piece band, cornet, guitar, and bass. The brother band. And that was everything. We'd go play for some of these old times, you know, they wanted, they wanted all this kind of, old kind of music. Of course, these young folks now, they don't look for that kind of music no more. But you can tell old people, they wanted walk, waltzes, mazookas, they wanted to shout us, and then around 11 o'clock that night, the long come old man there, he said, all right, he says, get yourself ready, he says, get yourself a sandwich and a beer, he says, because we're gonna put the lances on. And that was five parts. And that was something to play, cornet, guitar, and bass. We played it. We could go to town on that stuff. When did the blues come in? Well, the blues came in around, around 19, say around 1906. Real blues came in. W.C. Handy composed the St. Louis blues. I ain't heard one of them ever play the St. Louis blues right yet. Now the fellas that composed High Society, they said Buddy Bowles composed that. That's the Bologna, Alphonse Pico composed that piece. And, uh, the blues came in around 1906. We used to, uh, we used to play the blues, but not them kind of blues. But they're all, practically all the blues that you get now is always, it's on the same pattern all the way through. But you take, now you take this Boogie Woogie stuff, you can take it from one who knows. You know what that is? That's the old time color dance. That's when they used to get out there with their feet. Oh, I used to put their feet on board. They used to put it on. I mean put it on. And, uh, that's, that's Boogie Woogie. They call that Boogie Woogie now. But that's the same old tempo, same old method of playing, same rhythm, they used to play it like at L-I-V-A. What's that? L-I-V-A?
